content: Women who underwent biopsy with histological verification were included in the assessment of study quality using the QUADAS-2 tool. Studies that relied solely on cytological endpoints were excluded due to the lower sensitivity of cytology in detecting high-grade disease. A comprehensive search of databases, including the Wiley Cochrane Library, OvidSP Embase, OvidSP Global Health, and OvidSP Medline, was conducted on April 21-22, 2020, without restrictions on the start year. Search terms were derived from a detailed MEDLINE search strategy, focusing on cervical cancer, precancerous lesions, and diagnostic methods such as visual inspection, cytology, and HPV testing. All identified citations were imported into EndNote X9 software, and duplicates were removed. Abstracts were screened, and full-text copies of relevant publications were assessed for eligibility by one author, with data extraction verified by a second author for 30% of the studies. From 7,089 publications identified, 2,594 duplicates were removed, and 4,368 were excluded after abstract review, leaving 127 articles for full-text review. Ultimately, 31 articles met the inclusion criteria, with one additional eligible study published after the initial search. Most studies (61%) were conducted in Sub-Saharan Africa, with others in Asia, Latin America, North America, and Europe, involving a total of 19,112 women living with HIV (WLHIV). The majority of studies recruited WLHIV attending routine cervical cancer screening or HIV clinics, while a few focused on women with prior abnormal screening results. The median CD4+ T-cell count ranged from 271 cells/µL in studies conducted before widespread antiretroviral therapy (ART) introduction to 592 cells/µL in more recent studies where most participants were on ART. High-risk HPV (HR-HPV) prevalence ranged from 26% to 64%. Due to variability in study design, pooled accuracy estimates were not calculated. Sensitivity was lower in studies with less experienced visual inspection operators or inadequate quality control measures. Nineteen studies evaluated HPV DNA testing methods (e.g., Hybrid Capture II, GeneXpert, CareHPV) for detecting CIN2+/CIN3+ among 12,604 WLHIV. Sensitivity estimates for CIN2+ ranged from 76% to 97%, with similar findings for CIN3+. Sixteen studies assessed cervical cytology for CIN2+/CIN3+ detection among 8,366 WLHIV, using thresholds such as ASCUS+, LSIL+, and HSIL+. Conventional cytology was used in all but one study, which employed liquid-based cytology. Sensitivity and specificity varied widely, particularly for CIN2+ detection. Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) showed heterogeneous sensitivity and specificity across studies, with sensitivity decreasing in women aged 40 years and older. Positive predictive value (PPV) increased with age, corresponding to lower HR-HPV prevalence in older age groups. In two studies, HPV test sensitivity was higher in women recently initiating ART compared to those on prolonged ART, likely due to higher HR-HPV prevalence in the former group. Stratified analyses revealed that modifications to HPV testing, such as increasing the threshold for test positivity or using restricted genotype approaches, improved specificity with minimal impact on sensitivity. Cervical cytology performed well in settings with established laboratory infrastructure, with HSIL+ thresholds providing optimal sensitivity, specificity, and PPV. Adding a second test after an HPV-positive result reduced sensitivity but minimally improved specificity. Longitudinal studies evaluated cervical lesion outcomes following negative screening tests in WLHIV. Among women with normal cytology at baseline, the risk of CIN2+ or CIN3+ over follow-up visits was stratified by HIV and HR-HPV status. In one cohort, no cases of HSIL+ were diagnosed after three years of follow-up, though the endpoints were determined using cytology without histological confirmation. Regular evaluations every six months over five years provided additional insights into disease progression and risk factors.
